speaker: Elena Verna
title: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
question: In SaaS growth, why is relying mainly on paid ads, social, and SEO riskier than building earned product-led channels?
guest: When you rely on paid search, paid social, or even organic search, you are paying for access to somebody else's distribution and competing against other players inside their channel. All of those work on algorithms—and an algorithm can giveth, and an algorithm can taketh away at any point. Especially now, as search shifts toward AI interfaces that treat content like a database and give far less credit back to publishers, your cost of acquisition and competition in those channels only go up. By contrast, an earned channel—like virality, sharing loops, or user-generated content—is distribution you own that competitors cannot buy their way into. It is not cheap: it costs substantial product, engineering, and marketing resources to build. At Dropbox, over 50 percent of acquisition came through sharing files, which simultaneously created brand awareness and almost activated the recipient. If you don't diversify into earned channels, you leave your growth future in someone else's hands.

points.core: Rented channels depend on third-party algorithms that can abruptly cut off your traffic.
points.note: Accept: paid ads, social platforms, and SEO rely on someone else's distribution and opaque algorithms you do not control, which can take traffic away at any time. Do not credit: generic claims that SEO is dead without the platform-control/algorithm risk.

points.core: Competing inside third-party platforms continuously drives up your customer acquisition costs.
points.note: Accept: sharing rented distribution with competitors intensifies bidding and competition, pushing CAC steadily higher over time. Do not credit: merely saying ads cost money without the escalating competition/auction dynamic.

points.core: AI search interfaces increasingly absorb publisher content without sending direct referral traffic.
points.note: Accept: AI answer interfaces treat web content like a backend database and give less credit or click-through traffic back to original publishers, eroding organic search control. Do not credit: generic hype about AI changing marketing without the reduced-credit/referral mechanism.

points.core: Earned product loops create owned distribution that competitors cannot outbid with ad spend.
points.note: Accept: earned channels like sharing loops, virality, or user-generated content require heavy product/engineering investment to build, then deliver defensible distribution competitors cannot buy while pre-activating recipients. Do not credit: calling virality or word-of-mouth a free or effortless hack.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Relying mainly on paid ads, social, and SEO is riskier because those channels are rented, not owned. You depend on platforms whose incentives differ from yours: ad auctions get more expensive as competitors bid on the same audiences, algorithm changes can erase organic reach or search rankings overnight, and privacy and policy shifts can degrade targeting. AI-generated search answers are also reducing clicks to websites. Because every competitor can buy the same inventory, these channels offer no lasting advantage, and acquisition costs tend to rise as you exhaust the cheapest audiences. Growth also stops the moment spending stops, so the cost scales linearly with revenue.

Earned product-led channels, such as virality, referrals, user-generated content, integrations, collaboration invites, and word of mouth, are built into the product itself. Each new user can bring in more users, so growth compounds rather than being bought again each month. The marginal acquisition cost falls over time, the users who arrive are better qualified and retain better, and the loop is hard for competitors to copy because it depends on your product and user base.

The practical conclusion is to treat paid, social, and SEO as accelerants on top of a product-driven engine, not as the engine itself.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Relying mainly on paid ads, social media, and SEO places a SaaS company’s distribution in the hands of external gatekeepers whose incentives diverge from yours. Search engines and social platforms routinely change algorithms, throttle organic reach, and shift toward zero-click or AI-generated answers, which can erase traffic overnight, while content playbooks are easily copied by competitors. Paid acquisition carries a different fragility: growth scales linearly with spend, auctions saturate as rivals bid up the same audiences, and customer acquisition costs climb as creative fatigues, meaning momentum stalls the moment spending stops.

Earned product-led channels, such as collaborative invites, shared workflows, viral artifacts, and referrals, tie acquisition directly to product usage rather than rented attention. Because distribution happens as a byproduct of customers realizing value, active users compound reach at near-zero marginal cost. Prospects who first encounter a tool inside a colleague’s workflow also arrive with higher trust and clearer intent, driving stronger activation and retention while creating a durable growth moat competitors cannot simply outbid.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Paid ads, social, and SEO are rented channels. Someone else owns the platform and controls its rules, and many competitors are bidding for the same attention, so a SaaS company that depends on them carries several structural risks.

The first is cost. Ad auctions get more crowded over time, so customer acquisition cost tends to rise while each campaign brings in less. Growth then scales only with spending, and it stops when the budget does. The second is platform risk. A Google algorithm update, an AI-generated search answer that removes the need to click, a privacy change like Apple's tracking restrictions, or a policy shift can wipe out traffic overnight. The third is that competitors can copy these tactics by outbidding you or targeting the same keywords, so they rarely give you a lasting advantage.

Earned product-led channels work differently. Examples are viral invites, collaboration features, shareable outputs, referrals, integrations, and free tiers that turn into paid plans. Their reach grows with usage rather than spending. Each new user can bring in others at almost no extra cost, and the users who arrive tend to stay longer because they've already experienced the product's value. These loops compound, they're hard to copy, and you own them.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Relying mainly on paid ads, social media, and SEO is riskier because those are rented channels controlled by third-party platforms. Ad auctions become more expensive over time as competitors bid up customer acquisition costs, while sudden algorithm updates, privacy changes, or shifts in how search engines surface answers can cut traffic overnight. Growth from these channels is also mostly linear: the moment you reduce ad spend or slow down content production, acquisition drops.

Earned product-led channels—such as built-in collaboration, user referrals, shareable outputs, templates, and strong word-of-mouth—are far more durable because they are embedded in the product experience itself. Instead of paying repeatedly for attention, each active user naturally exposes new prospects to the product simply by using it. That creates a compounding growth loop that lowers acquisition costs as you scale, attracts higher-intent users who already see the product’s value in context, and insulates the business from external platform volatility.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Relying mainly on paid ads, social, and SEO makes SaaS growth vulnerable to decisions outside your control. Ad auctions can drive up customer acquisition costs, and changes to social feeds or search rankings can cut traffic overnight. Paid traffic also tends to drop as soon as you stop spending.

Earned product-led channels turn customer value into distribution. When users invite teammates, share something they made, or recommend the product, their everyday use introduces it to potential customers. Those introductions come with context and often trust, and they can compound as new users repeat the behavior.

Product-led channels still depend on a product people find valuable enough to share. When that behavior is already happening, paid and organic marketing can amplify it, giving the business more than one way to grow.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Paid ads, social, and SEO depend on platforms that control what it costs to reach customers and who sees you. Ad prices can rise, and a feed or search algorithm change can cut traffic overnight. When you stop buying ads, the traffic they deliver usually stops too.

Earned product-led channels grow through customers using and sharing the product. When someone invites a teammate or shares a report with a client, a potential customer experiences the product’s value firsthand. If those people become active users and bring in others, acquisition can compound as the customer base grows, with less dependence on ad budgets or platform decisions. That advantage depends on sharing being a natural, useful part of the product.
